Choosing CNC milling, turning or 5-axis machining

A shaft or sleeve will usually start with turning. A housing with pockets and flat mounting faces is more likely to need milling. Angled features or access to several faces may call for a multi-axis setup. Some parts need a combination; send the drawing so we can review the sequence.

Compare the processes by geometry
Process	Typical geometry	Drawing requirements
CNC turning	Rotational features such as a shaft, sleeve, disc or fitting, often arranged around an axis. Turning capabilities.	Define the datum axis, diameters, shoulders, grooves, threads and runout if required. Confirm whether cross-holes, flats or slots need secondary milling.
CNC milling	Block-like or irregular forms with pockets, slots, holes, contours and planar mounting faces. Milling capabilities.	Define datum faces, pocket depth, hole patterns and positional relationships. Confirm stock, clamping surfaces, setups and inspection records.
Multi-axis machining	Features distributed over several faces, angled faces or areas that need different tool approaches. Multi-axis capabilities.	Define common datums, face-to-face and angular relationships. Review tool access, workholding and sequence against the model.

Some turned parts also need milling, for example to add flats or cross-holes. A housing may require another setup to reach an angled face. The machining sequence must preserve the relationships between critical features, so send both a 3D model and the controlling 2D drawing.

Accuracy depends on the feature

Accuracy is assessed at the feature level. Geometry and material affect the achievable limit, together with the setup and datum strategy. Finishing and the measurement method also affect acceptance. State the tolerance and datum for each critical interface so its machining and inspection can be planned.

Files for a process recommendation
A 3D model and the controlling 2D drawing revision.
Material grade and condition, or the functional requirement if still undecided.
Quantity for the first order and expected repeat pattern, if known.
Critical datums, fits, surface requirements and required inspection records.
Finish, packaging and required arrival date, with any standards or approvals identified.

Use the RFQ checklist to organize those details. We review your drawing before confirming the machining process and quoting a price and schedule.
